# Index Cards {#sec-index-cards}

The wall had shown me the chapters.
What I needed, I decided, was a way to see the claims.

So I bought index cards, the plain white kind, and a shoebox to keep them in.
One claim per card.
On the front, the claim, in as few words as it would go: *the shop in chapter four made the dash fashionable.*
On the back, the chapter, the page, and the sentence that made the claim, copied out by hand.

It took most of a month.
Eleven chapters hold more claims than you would think, and most of them are small: a date, a street, which apprentice married whose daughter.
I wrote them all.
The shoebox filled, and I bought a second shoebox and labeled both, and for the first time in a year I felt like someone running a project rather than someone being run by one.

The cards worked the way the wall had worked, which is to say at first.
When I changed a sentence, I found its card and changed that too.
When I couldn't find its card, I wrote a new one, and later I found the old one, and then there were two cards for one claim, disagreeing in my own handwriting.
Every round of chapter four against chapter nine went through the shoebox now.
Each round took twice as long, and I could prove it.

One card fell behind the radiator.
I didn't notice.
A shoebox does not tell you what it is missing.

I found it in March, when the heating went off and I could get my arm down behind the pipes.
It was the card for the shop in chapter nine.
It said what chapter nine said, which by then nothing else did.

I put it back in the box.
I am not sure where.

A spreadsheet cannot fall behind a radiator, which was most of its appeal.
I typed every card into one, a row per claim, with columns for the chapter, the page, the claim, and the sentence.
When I finished it had three hundred and twelve rows.
I added a column for status, and the status was a color.
Green, for a note that still matched its sentence.
Yellow, for check.
Red, for contradicts.

That lasted about a week.
Then I needed orange, for contradicts but I like it.

Orange was mostly chapter four.

Four colors are more than anyone can hold in their head at eleven at night, so I added a tab called Legend, with one cell of each color and what it meant.
Then I put a note at the top of Legend explaining the orange.

I kept the spreadsheet for most of a year, and I got very good at it.
I could sort by color, filter by chapter, and tell you on any evening how many rows were yellow.
What I could not tell you was whether the green rows were still green.
The spreadsheet knew what I had typed into it.
It did not know what the chapters said.
Every time I changed a sentence I had to go and find its row, and every time I forgot, the row stayed green about a sentence that no longer existed.

I write software for a living.
I mention it here because it took me this long to mention it to myself.

The script was forty lines, written on a Sunday.
It read each note, found the sentence the note was about, and complained when the sentence had moved or changed.
That was all it did.
It had no opinion about the dash.
It did not know there was a dash.

I ran it that evening.
It found fourteen contradictions.

I assumed it was broken.
The book had one contradiction, and I knew it by heart.
I went through the fourteen one at a time, looking for the bug.

It wasn't broken.

Some of the fourteen were the two shops, in other clothes.
Some had nothing to do with them: a date in chapter three that chapter eight had quietly moved by a decade, a schoolmaster who was Scottish in chapter five and not in chapter ten.
Three were things I had fixed in the spreadsheet and never in the book.

Hedda's one-on-one was that Thursday.
For the first time, I spent the twenty-six minutes not rehearsing.

"How's the book?" she asked.

"I'm building something for chapter four," I said.

She looked at me a moment longer than the four minutes usually allowed.
Then she said, "Good," and wrote it down.

Two weeks later her document was open on her monitor when I came in, and the line under Other had changed for the first time since I had known it.

*Book: ch. 4 (tool)*

Three years, and the line had moved seven characters.

The script grew.
Scripts do.
It needed to know which chapters to read, and in what order, and which notes to leave alone because I had not decided about them yet, so it grew a configuration file.
The configuration file filled with options I added at night and could not account for in the morning, so it grew a second configuration file, to explain the first.

I spent the evenings with the script that I used to spend with chapter four.
They were better evenings.
The script told me when I was wrong, which chapter four had stopped doing years before, and it told me in under a second.

One night it reported the two shops again, as it did every night, along with everything else, and I looked up from it at the wall, still pinned with six chapters, and at the shoeboxes underneath, and I saw what I had been looking at for three years.

The book had never failed at the sentences.
Its claims lived only in sentences, scattered across eleven chapters, with nothing holding them together.

I took the chapters down that weekend.
The pins left holes in the plaster, in pairs.

Two weeks later Hedda asked how the book was.

"I'm building something for chapter four," I said.

It was still true.
It was getting truer.

content.text:
Chapter three, Index Cards, is written in `manuscript/sections/index-cards.qmd`. All five gates pass, in order. Nothing is committed.

**The chapter**

- **The cards:** the cards and shoeboxes come first. The card behind the radiator turns out to be chapter nine's shop. I kept your sentence as you wrote it, "It said what chapter nine said, which by then nothing else did," and the chapter doesn't explain it.
- **The spreadsheet:** it has 312 rows and runs green, yellow, red, then orange ("contradicts but I like it"). Then come the Legend tab and the note at the top of Legend explaining the orange, and nothing more is said about it.
- **The script:** it's forty lines, written on a Sunday, and finds fourteen contradictions, which Cy assumes is a bug. It isn't.
- **Hedda:** her second answer lands when the script starts. She says "Good," writes it down, and her line changes to *Book: ch. 4 (tool)*, followed by "Three years, and the line had moved seven characters." After that the script grows two configuration files, the second explaining the first.
- **The point:** near the end it says, once, that the book never failed at the sentences and its claims lived only in sentences. It isn't repeated. The chapter closes part one with your answer to Hedda as a refrain, which mirrors how chapter one ends.
- **The name:** the script is never named.

**Other changes**

- **Sidecar:** I added two guidance notes: the main point is said once, and the script stays unnamed here. I added `@count` marks for both "eleven chapters" and "Eleven chapters" and removed the old `@todo`. The `@bind` lines were already right.
- **Spec:**
  - `#notes-escalate` now carries your new material.
  - `#people-who-ask` used to say the line "survives every copy." It now says the line survives until the second answer, then changes to "Book: ch. 4 (tool)". Without that change the spec would contradict the chapter.
  - `#claims-in-sentences` now says the point is stated once, near the end.
- **Trail:** I added a breadcrumb for each of those three sections, pointing at your message. This session isn't captured yet, so `trail --check` flags them as advisory until you run `quirework provenance ingest claude`.
- **Wrapping:** `dev check` first failed on line wrapping. I ran `quirework text wrap` on the chapter and the spec. That tool asks for wrapping to be committed on its own, so you may want to split the commit.

**Needs your judgment**

- **Length:** the chapter is about 1,020 words. The guidance allows about 1,500, so all the slack Two Shops left over, and about 280 words more, is unused. I didn't pad it, given rule 4. If you want it longer, the cards and the fourteen contradictions are the natural places to grow.
- **Invented details:** I made up three of the fourteen contradictions so the list feels real: a date moved by a decade between chapters three and eight, a schoolmaster who is Scottish in chapter five and not in ten, and three fixes made in the spreadsheet but never in the book. I also invented the closing image of pin holes left in pairs. Cut any of these if you'd rather not have them.
- **Last line:** the chapter ends on "It was getting truer." That may be one beat too cute.
- **When the script gets its name:** you said "the next chapter," which would be Otto. The spec has Otto naming it in The Name, which is chapter five. I only made sure this chapter doesn't name it, and left the spec saying The Name.
- **A wrapping quirk:** the wrapper splits *Book: ch. 4 (tool)* after "ch.", as it already did in chapter one. It still renders on one line.

content:
Good. "Three years, and the line had moved seven characters" is the best sentence in part one.

Four things.

"I write software for a living" isn't true. I'm a documentation engineer: I write about software for a living, which is close enough that I should have seen this sooner. Make the line say that, keep the next one as it is, and put my job in the guide's cast list so nobody makes me a programmer again.

Cut "It was getting truer." End on "It was still true." The reader can do the rest.

You're right about the name. It's The Name, chapter five, as the spec says. I miscounted, which is on brand.

Keep all three invented contradictions and the pin holes. The schoolmaster who is Scottish in chapter five and not in ten is now one of my favourite people. Favorite. US.

Length is fine. Short is a rule, not a shortfall. It's new text, so one commit is fine. Commit it, then we're done for today.

content.text:
I made all four changes and committed them as `23c31f4`, "Write chapter three, Index Cards". All five checks passed first.

- **Your job:** the line now reads "I write about software for a living." The next line is unchanged. The cast list in `AGENTS.md` now says you're a documentation engineer and not a programmer.
- **Ending:** the chapter now ends on "It was still true."
- **The name:** no change needed. The spec already says The Name, chapter five.
- **Length:** I added your line to house rule 4: a chapter's word count is a ceiling, not a target, and short is a rule, not a shortfall.

The three invented contradictions and the pin holes stay as they are.

This session still needs capturing with `quirework provenance ingest claude`. The three breadcrumbs I added today point at it, and until it's captured, `trail --check` keeps flagging them as warnings. They don't fail the check.
